_readme: The story-time corpus (P3-8). Written from specs/bible.md section 7 as the specification, not recorded from archetype/bible/storytime.py: every answer here is what that document says must happen, and a disagreement is a bug in one of them rather than a fixture to re-record. Read by tests/test_storytime.py. Each case is (events, precedes edges, the three answers), which is the whole input and the whole output of a pure function - there is no database here and no clock. An event is {id, name?, sort_key?, era?, label?}; 'sort_key' absent means the event carries none, which is not the same as zero. 'edges' are [from, to] pairs meaning 'from comes before to'. 'order' is the exact list, in order; 'unplaced' is a set stated as a list in the events' own order; 'contradictions' each state a kind ('cycle' or 'sort_key_inversion' - there are no others) and the events involved, compared as a set for a cycle because the member a cycle is listed from is an implementation detail while its membership is not. 'eras' is the era ranking of section 7's last paragraph, where null means an era nobody has placed - which is not a contradiction. Absent 'eras' means the case says nothing about eras.

cases.name: nothing at all
cases.why: A bible with no events is the state every project starts in, and the answer is three empty lists rather than an error.

cases.name: a label alone does not place an event
cases.why: Section 7: a label is for reading, not for sorting. It is the tray, not the timeline.

events.name: The flood
events.label: the third night of the flood

cases.name: sort keys alone order two events
cases.why: A key places an event without any edge; the smaller comes first.

cases.name: an edge alone orders two events with no keys at all
cases.why: This is the case D9 exists for: a writer who will never give a number can still say what came first.

cases.name: an edge and keys that agree
cases.why: The ordinary case, and the one that must report nothing.

cases.name: an edge wins over the keys, and the inversion is reported
cases.why: Tiebreak rule 1: a constraint a person typed outranks a number they typed. The pair is still ordered by the edge - this is step 6 of the acceptance run.

cases.name: an inversion does not stop the rest of the events being ordered
cases.why: A contradiction never costs the graph. The unrelated event keeps its place by its key.

cases.name: an unkeyed event placed by an edge comes after every keyed one it is not ordered against
cases.why: Tiebreak rule 3, stated as data. 'c' has a key and no edge; 'b' has an edge and no key, so nobody said when it happens.

cases.name: keyed, edge-placed, and unplaced together
cases.why: The three forms of section 7's table in one case. 'd' has neither a key nor an edge and is the tray - step 7 of the acceptance run.

cases.name: a two-event cycle is reported and both events stay in the order
cases.why: Section 7: a cycle is reported as a cycle and everything outside it is still ordered. Nothing is dropped - every event is in exactly one of order and unplaced.

cases.name: a three-event cycle costs only itself, and the edge that closes it also inverts
cases.why: The events on either side of the loop are still ordered around it, which is what makes the loop findable. The closing edge runs from key 12 back to key 10, so it is an inversion as well: the two kinds are independent and one must not mask the other.

cases.name: an event said to precede itself is a cycle of one
cases.why: It is the same mistake at its smallest, and reporting it as anything else would need a third contradiction kind.

cases.name: a diamond orders its two middles by their keys
cases.why: The edges leave 'b' and 'c' unordered against each other, so tiebreak rule 2 decides - and rule 1 still holds both against 'a' and 'd'.

cases.name: two unkeyed chains fall back on the order the events were given in
cases.why: Tiebreak rule 4. Nothing here is sorted by name or by anything a person did not say - the fallback is stable and nothing more.

cases.name: the same link twice is one constraint
cases.why: Two identical rows can exist across a delete and a re-create; they say the same thing once.

cases.name: an edge naming an event that is not here is ignored
cases.why: The caller's live predicate decides which events exist; an edge to a deleted one is not a constraint against this graph, and it must not place the event at the near end either.

cases.name: eras rank by the least sort key among their members
cases.why: Section 7's last paragraph. 'Before' holds the smaller key even though its other member is larger, and an era whose members carry no key has no rank - which is not a contradiction.

cases.name: an era is a grouping and carries no ordering power
cases.why: Two events in the same era are ordered by the same rules as any other two - the era name never enters the comparison.

cases.name: a negative and a fractional key order like any other
cases.why: sort_key is a float on purpose, so an event can be inserted between two others without renumbering (section 11).

cases.name: a cycle and an inversion in the same graph are both reported
cases.why: The two kinds are independent, and one must not mask the other.
